sections.title: Objective type questions: each has two parts of 1 mark (fill in the blanks, true/false, one word or phrase, match).

questions.q: Answer in short phrases: How was the dispensing of education organised during the medieval period in India? Write two facts.
questions.answer: Makhtabs gave school education and madrasas gave higher education; they were supported by donations and rulers and nobles and followed a curriculum of traditional and rational sciences.

questions.q: Explain any two characteristic features of Ghatikas in short phrases.
questions.answer: They were colleges attached to temples that gave Brahmanical education in Sanskrit, open only to the upper (twice-born) castes.

questions.q: Match two items given in Column A to Column B (the rest are distracters): Varanasi – Centre of learning; Yashastilaka – Jain literature; Upanayana – Maurya; Education – Architecture. Give two correct pairs.
questions.answer: Varanasi – centre of learning; Yashastilaka – Jain literature.

questions.q: Mark true or false: (a) Varanasi was not a centre of learning. (b) Yashastilak was used for educational purposes by Jains.
questions.answer: (a) False – it was a centre of learning (medicine was taught). (b) True.

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: In ancient India education was a matter of ______ concern. The aim was development of the pupil's overall ______.
Answer in short phrases: Mention any two sources which gave grants for the maintenance of Buddhist monasteries during the Gupta period.
questions.answer: Kings and the rich mercantile class (merchants).

questions.q: Mark true or false: (a) The Dharmashastras and Smritis tried to fix duties of each caste. (b) Mathas were supported by Jains.
questions.answer: (a) True. (b) False – mathas were supported by Brahmins.

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: Learning in the Gurukul began with the ______ ceremony. The relationship was called the ______ parampara.
Answer in a phrase: (a) What was the basis of the Indian medical system in ancient times? (b) Name the two works used by Jains for teaching.
questions.answer: (a) Three elements – air (vayu), mucus (kapha) and bile (pitta). (b) Adipurana and Yashastilaka.

questions.q: Mark true or false: (a) Education was in the concurrent list from 1976. (b) Kothari Commission was set up in 1986.
Answer in a phrase: (a) Name two famous madrasas of medieval India. (b) What was the main feature of Muslim education?
questions.answer: (a) Muizzi and Firuzi madrasas (or Gawan's at Bidar). (b) Traditional in spirit and theological in content.

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: The Indian Universities Act was passed in ______. Universities were set up in Bombay, Madras and Calcutta in ______.
Mark true or false: (a) Wood's Despatch proposed universities in three cities. (b) The 1813 Charter Act set aside Rs 10 lakh.
Answer in a phrase: (a) What are the thrust areas of elementary education in the 1986 policy? (b) What does RMSA aim at?
questions.answer: (a) Universal access and enrolment, universal retention up to 14, and improved quality. (b) Universal access to and quality of secondary education.

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: Literacy rate in 2011 was ______ per cent. The age group for adult education is ______ years.

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in about 25 words.

questions.q: Explain the main changes which came in education during the medieval period.
questions.answer: The Islamic system was introduced with maktabs and madrasas under royal patronage; the curriculum had traditional and rational sciences; Akbar and Humayun added mathematics, geography, accountancy and administration; Persian was taught and works were translated from Sanskrit.

or.q: Explain about the proliferation of Islamic institutions in India in the medieval period.
or.answer: Maktabs for schools and madrasas for higher learning were set up by rulers and nobles, scholars, mosques, tombs and Sufi hospices; famous ones were Muizzi, Nasiri, Firuzi, Gawan's and Abul Fazl's.

questions.q: Examine the spirit and content of Muslim education during the medieval period. Write any two points.
questions.answer: It was traditional in spirit and theological in content; lessons were memorised, discussed and written out; the curriculum had traditional (law, tradition, history, literature) and rational (logic, philosophy, medicine, mathematics, astronomy) sciences.

or.q: How was the curriculum divided in two categories during the medieval period?
or.answer: Into traditional sciences (Manqulat) and rational sciences (Maqulat).

questions.q: Name two universities from ancient India, one located in Bihar and the other in the North-Western region.
questions.answer: Nalanda (Bihar) and Taxila (Takshashila) in the North-West.

questions.q: Examine the activities of the Indian Universities Act of 1904.
questions.answer: It enabled universities to undertake teaching (not only examinations), inspection of colleges and measures for qualitative improvement in higher education.

questions.q: Explain the significance of higher education in the development of India (any two points).
questions.answer: Higher education produces skilled manpower, leaders and researchers needed for scientific and industrial development and promotes personality, reasoning and learning; it is highly subsidised by the State.

or.q: Explain any two challenges faced by higher education in India.
or.answer: Uneven development and poor facilities in most colleges; low enrolment of the 18–20 age group, especially women, SC/ST and rural youth.

questions.q: How does the Right to Education Act help in the spread of education in India?
questions.answer: It makes elementary education free and compulsory for children aged 6–14 in a neighbourhood school; local authorities identify drop-outs and admit them in age-appropriate classes with special training.

or.q: Explain how school management or local authorities can help in implementing the RTE Act.
or.answer: They identify drop-outs and out-of-school children above six years and admit them to classes appropriate to their age after special training.

questions.q: Mention names of three countries/regions from which scholars were called to teach in Indian madrasas.
Why were guilds important in the Mauryan period for education?
questions.answer: They became centres of technical education fostering mining, metallurgy, carpentry, weaving and dyeing and patronised astronomy for navigation.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 40–50 words.

questions.q: Explain the importance of vocational education given at the senior secondary stage.
questions.answer: Vocational education is a distinct stream at the senior secondary stage that prepares students for various occupations, reduces unemployment and gives skills; ITIs train in 57 engineering and 50 non-engineering trades and the National Skill Development Mission supports it, though enrolment has remained marginal.

or.q: Explain any three developments in the Indian education system.
or.answer: Free and compulsory education for 6–14 (RTE), Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan and RMSA to universalise elementary and secondary education, and National Literacy Mission and open learning for adults and drop-outs.

questions.q: Mention any three features of the education system under the Mughals.
questions.answer: Education through pathshalas, vidyapeeths, makhtabs and madrasas; temples and mosques as centres of elementary education teaching Sanskrit and Persian, supported by donations; Akbar added accountancy, public administration and geometry, gave grants and built a workshop; no formal women's education.

questions.q: Describe the education system under the Gupta period (Buddhist monasteries).
questions.answer: Buddhist monasteries admitted students for ten years, taught orally and later from texts, had libraries and copied manuscripts, took students from China and South-East Asia, were supported by kings and rich merchants, and Nalanda became famous all over Asia.

questions.q: Write about the impact of English education.
questions.answer: English was encouraged to create clerks and babus; it became a common link language, brought ideas of freedom, democracy and equality that gave rise to national consciousness and produced leaders and reformers, but it was uneven and neglected mass education.

questions.q: Explain the role of Wood's Despatch of 1854.
questions.answer: It stated the objective of spreading European arts, sciences, philosophy and literature through English or modern Indian languages and proposed universities in Bombay, Madras and Calcutta, grants-in-aid, teacher training and women's education; the universities were set up in 1857.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 150–200 words.

questions.q: Briefly describe the development of education in ancient India.
questions.answer: In the Vedic period education was oral, in Gurukuls through the guru–shishya parampara, beginning with Upanayana and for the upper castes. Guilds became centres of technical education in the Mauryan period, and Ayurveda developed. Under the Guptas Buddhist monasteries (Nalanda) and Jain institutions flourished with grants from kings and merchants; under Harsha education was given in temples, monasteries and universities such as Taxila and Nalanda; ghatikas gave Brahmanical education in Sanskrit to the upper castes. The aim was the all-round development of personality and the training of the mind.

questions.q: Discuss the steps taken in education with the establishment of the Delhi Sultanate and under the Mughals.
questions.answer: Under the Sultans Islamic education was introduced: makhtabs and madrasas with a traditional and rational curriculum; Sikandar Lodi invited Sheikh Abdullah and Azizullah to introduce philosophy and logic. Under the Mughals education spread through pathshalas, maktabs and madrasas; Humayun introduced mathematics, astronomy and geography; Akbar added accountancy, public administration and geometry, gave grants and tried a secular and scientific system; translations from Sanskrit to Persian were made; women were taught at home.

questions.q: Elaborate the development of education from 1813 to 1904.
questions.answer: The Charter Act of 1813 set aside Rs one lakh for education. The Orientalist–Anglicist debate ended with Macaulay's Minute and Bentinck's Resolution (1835): European literature and science, with English as the official language. Wood's Despatch (1854) proposed universities, grants-in-aid, teacher training and women's education; universities of Bombay, Madras and Calcutta were set up in 1857, Punjab (1882) and Allahabad (1887). Curzon's conference (1901) led to the Indian Universities Act of 1904.

questions.q: Discuss the measures taken in independent India to spread education and eradicate illiteracy.
questions.answer: Education was made a concurrent subject (1976); the Constitution provides free and compulsory education to age 14; the National Policy on Education (1968, 1986) set thrust areas; Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan (2001) and RMSA expanded elementary and secondary education; the 86th Amendment (2002) and the RTE Act (2010) made education a fundamental right for 6–14; the National Literacy Mission targets the 15–35 age group; Navodaya Vidyalayas, open and distance learning (NIOS, IGNOU) and vocational and technical institutions (ITIs, IITs, IIMs) were set up. Literacy rose from 18.3% (1951) to 74% (2011).
